d.title: The '1 token is about 4 characters' rule, measured on six samples
d.caption: The claim holds for English prose and nothing else. Measured, prose comes to 4.43 characters per token — close enough — while JSON is 2.77 and **UUIDs are 1.95**, so an id-heavy payload costs more than twice what the rule predicts. The last row is the one that bites internationally: the same French text is 73 tokens in cl100k and 57 in o200k, so switching tokeniser changed the bill by 22% with no change to the text.

d.title: finish_reason, and what each value obliges you to do
d.caption: This field is the difference between a truncated answer and a complete one, and code that ignores it treats the two identically. `length` is the one that silently corrupts results — a JSON response cut at `max_tokens` is unparseable, and a prose answer cut there just looks like a short answer. **Never retry `content_filter` blindly**; surface it.

d.title: Reserve output space; do not leave it as a remainder
d.caption: The pattern that works inverts the usual one. Decide how much output the feature needs, subtract it from the window with a margin, and let the prompt builder fill whatever is left — dropping the lowest-priority material when it runs out. The figure to log is `chunks_dropped`: **a retrieval system that silently drops half its context is one whose recall measurements no longer describe what the model saw**, and that disconnect is behind a large share of "retrieval is good but answers are bad" investigations.

nodes.label: Reserve the output first
nodes.sub: what the feature needs, plus margin

nodes.label: Drop by priority when it runs out

d.title: A stop sequence truncates the response; it does not stop the generation
d.caption: The model produced 30 tokens in every row below. The stop string decides how many of them you are *shown* — and you are **billed for all 30 regardless**. With `stop=","` one token survives out of thirty. The third row is the other half of the trap: a stop string the model never emits does nothing at all, and generation simply runs to `max_tokens`.

d.title: What a bias number is worth, in odds
d.caption: A bias is added to the logit, so it multiplies the token's odds by `exp(bias)` — which makes the scale readable. **−100 is a ban** (odds × 4×10⁻⁴⁴, rank 50,257). −5 is strong discouragement that is still reachable. +5 is usually decisive and +10 is effectively forced. And +100 is indistinguishable from +10 at any precision you can observe, so reaching for a bigger number past +10 buys nothing.

d.title: The id is not the word, and that is the whole disappointment
d.caption: `logit_bias` maps **ids to numbers**, and biasing `' blue'` leaves every other spelling of blue untouched. Seven forms of one word, six distinct ids, and one — `' bluish'` — that is not a single token at all, so no bias can reach it: you would have to bias `' blu'`, which also suppresses every other word starting that way. The one place the parameter is unbeatable is a single-token classifier: bias everything but your labels to −100, set `max_tokens=1`, and the answer is guaranteed to be a label, with its logprob as a free confidence score.

d.title: What the seed fixes, and what it leaves alone
d.caption: A seed fixes the pseudo-random draw, so three runs at `seed=42` return the same sentence byte for byte while three unseeded runs return three different ones. What it cannot fix is anything upstream of the draw: the logits themselves. Those depend on the weights, the serving stack and — as §03 measures — how your request was batched, none of which is in your request.

nodes.label: But batching moves the logits
nodes.sub: and you do not control it

nodes.label: Nor does a new model version care

d.title: Batch composition moves the logits, and no seed reaches it
d.caption: Left-padding the same prompt inside a batch of 2 changed **nothing** — 0.000e+00 across all 50,257 logits, because the attention mask did its job. Changing the batch *size* did: at batch 4 and 16 the logits differ from the solo run by 1.984e-04. That is fp non-associativity in the reduction order, not a bug, and it is enough to flip the argmax whenever the top two tokens are within that distance.

d.title: If correctness needs the same bytes twice, stop asking twice
d.caption: `system_fingerprint` identifies the backend configuration, and the contract is simple: **if it changes, do not expect the same output even with the same seed**. Which points at the real fix. A system whose correctness depends on an LLM returning identical bytes should store the output the first time, key it on everything that could change it, and serve the stored copy. Everything else is an attempt to make a hosted, batched, floating-point system behave like a pure function.

Serve the stored copy
nodes.sub: now it is a pure function

d.title: A Pydantic class is a JSON Schema you are billed for
d.caption: `FruitList` becomes a schema with `$defs`, `properties`, `required` and `type` on every field — and that schema **costs 137 tokens on every request it is sent with**. Which is the thing nobody counts: a comfortably documented model with a dozen fields and descriptions is a fixed per-call tax, paid on every turn of every conversation, for information that never changes.

nodes.label: Field descriptions cost too
nodes.sub: they are part of the schema

d.title: Strict mode has no optional fields
d.caption: OpenAI's structured outputs accept only a subset of JSON Schema, and the restriction that changes your code is this one: **every property must appear in `required`**. There is no optional field. What you write instead is a field that is required but nullable — `anyOf: [string, null]` with a default — so the model must emit the key and may emit `null` as its value. The distinction matters downstream, because 'absent' and 'present but null' are different things to the code that reads it.

nodes.label: The model must emit the key
Absent and null are not the same
nodes.sub: to the code that reads it

d.title: A forced tool call is structured output with a different name
d.caption: Anthropic has no `response_format`, and the documented approach is to define a tool whose input schema is the shape you want and force the model to call it — at which point **the arguments the model produces *are* your structured response**, conforming for exactly the reason function-call arguments always do. The pattern generalises: any provider with function calling already has structured output.

nodes.label: Define a tool
nodes.sub: its input schema is your shape

d.title: The schema removes the shape failures, not the wrong answers
d.caption: Structured output guarantees `calories` is an integer. It does not guarantee the integer is right — **a banana at 3,000 calories satisfies the schema perfectly**, and so does a `confidence` of 1.0 on an answer the model invented. The point of the schema is that it clears away the failures that are about *shape*, so your validation code can be about *meaning*. Code doing both jobs usually does the second one badly.

nodes.label: Not that the value is right
Code doing both does the second badly

d.title: A tool definition does two different jobs
d.caption: The model reads one JSON object and uses its halves for different decisions. **Whether** to call and **which** one comes almost entirely from the `name` and `description` — a retrieval problem in miniature, matching intent against short text. **What arguments** to produce comes from the `parameters` schema and is enforced exactly as structured output is, which is why an `enum` on `unit` means the model cannot invent `kelvin`. Vague descriptions cause wrong-tool bugs; loose schemas cause wrong-argument bugs, and they are fixed in different places.

nodes.label: Two bugs, two different fixes
nodes.sub: which is why this split matters

d.title: tool_choice, and the job each setting is for
d.caption: Four settings, and the two middle ones are the ones people never reach for. `"none"` keeps the tools *visible* while forbidding the call, which is how you get the model to talk **about** its tools or to force a summary turn after a sequence of calls. `"required"` is for a turn that is meaningless without data — a router or a lookup step — where letting the model answer from memory is the failure.
cells: the model decides whether and which
a router, or a lookup step

d.title: Tools are a fixed tax on every request in the conversation
d.caption: One definition is 85 tokens, and definitions are resent on **every** turn because the model is stateless. Twenty tools is 1,700 tokens before the user has said anything — and at $2.50 per million input tokens, 100,000 requests with twenty tools is $425, or **$4,250 once each conversation runs ten turns**. Which is the argument for routing to a small tool subset rather than attaching the whole catalogue.

d.title: The model's tool call is a request, not an instruction
d.caption: The schema guarantees the arguments are well-typed. It guarantees nothing about whether they are **safe**, and those values arrived from a model that was reading user-supplied text. This is where prompt injection stops being a content problem and becomes an action problem: if a tool reads a web page, an email or a retrieved document, that text is in the context and can contain instructions. The defence is always at step 3 — your code authorises the action, not the model.

nodes.sub: a page, an email, a document
